Bayesian safety signal detection with bssd

Source: vignettes/bssd.Rmd
bssd.Rmd
library(bssd)

Introduction

The safety of a study drug is often monitored while the treatment assignment of an ongoing trial is still blinded. The blinded data show the adverse events of special interest, but not the treatment groups of the subjects. bssd computes the posterior probability that the risk of the event is higher on the study drug than on placebo (control) from such data, with published Bayesian methods. Several of these methods were computed by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. bssd computes all posterior distributions by numerical integration, so the results do not depend on a random seed, and they are fast enough for simulation studies of the operating characteristics (sim_oc()).

Models and functions

Model Function Blinded data Tested quantity Article
BDRIBS(1) (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018; Duncan, 2026) bdribs_post() number of subjects with the event and total exposure time rate ratio vignette("bdribs1")
BDRIBS(2) (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2018; Duncan, 2026) bdribs_post() number of subjects with the event and total time at risk rate ratio vignette("bdribs2")
BINBETA (Ball and Schnell, 2016) binbeta_post() numbers of subjects and of subjects with the event study drug proportion or ratio vignette("binbeta")
MULTIBIN (Goren et al., 2020) multibin_post() the same, for each of several studies common rate ratio vignette("binbeta")
CANARY (Gould and Wang, 2017) canary_post() total event count, with external control data ratio, difference or odds ratio vignette("canary")
EXP_BERN (Duncan, 2026) expbern_post() event indicator and follow-up time of each subject rate ratio vignette("expbern")
LL_BERN (Duncan, 2026) llbern_post() event indicator and follow-up time of each subject ratio of the cumulative incidences at t_star vignette("llbern")
EXPTIME (Schnell and Ball, 2016) exptime_post() number of events and follow-up time of each subject study drug rate or rate ratio vignette("exptime")
MAPBERN (Brock et al., 2023) mapbern_post(), map_beta() event indicator and time at risk of each subject, historical control arms ratio of the event probabilities vignette("mapbern")
BDRIBS monitoring (Waterhouse et al., 2022) bdribs_grid(), pooled_ratio() as BDRIBS, for grids of data and pooled trials rate ratio vignette("bdribs-monitoring")

Each article describes the model and its numerical integration, with examples and comparisons with MCMC or with the published results.

The study drug and placebo are randomized in the ratio \(k:1\). The models differ in what they assume about the treatment assignment. In EXP_BERN, LL_BERN, BINBETA, MULTIBIN, EXPTIME and MAPBERN, each subject is on study drug with probability \(k / (k + 1)\) (simple randomization); in BDRIBS the exposure is divided between the arms in the ratio \(k:1\), and in CANARY the arm sizes are fixed at their expected values (Gould and Wang, 2017). The prior of the placebo parameters must be informative in all models (for example, from historical placebo data), because the blinded data alone do not separate the two arms.

A signal is declared when the posterior probability that the tested quantity exceeds its critical value is larger than a threshold, for example \(P(RR > rr_0 \mid \mathrm{data}) > \mathrm{cutoff}\) for a relative risk \(RR\). The defaults are \(rr_0 = 1\) and \(\mathrm{cutoff} = 0.95\). BINBETA, EXPTIME and MAPBERN can instead test the study drug proportion or rate against a critical value.

signal_count() gives the smallest event count with a signal for a number of subjects (the boundaries of Ball and Schnell, 2016, and the control charts of Gould and Wang, 2017), count_oc() the exact probability that the count reaches it, and elicit_prior() the parameters of a prior from two quantiles.

Example with aggregate data

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has a 2:1 randomization, a background event rate of 0.011 per patient-year on placebo, and 540 patient-years of blinded exposure. The BDRIBS model sets the prior of the rate ratio \(r\) through the probability \(p = r k / (r k + 1)\) that a subject with the event is on the study drug, with \(p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\) (p_prior; vignette("bdribs1")). The screening analysis of the article treats the background rate as known, which corresponds to pt_hp = Inf. With the uniform prior for \(p\), the posterior probabilities for 8 and 9 events are

ex2 <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
ex2$bssd <- mapply(function(y, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, details = FALSE)$prob
}, ex2$y, ex2$rr0)
ex2$published <- c(0.622, 0.434, 0.756, 0.584)
knitr::kable(ex2[, c("y", "rr0", "bssd", "published")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Events", "rr0", "bssd", "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
Events rr0 bssd Mukhopadhyay et al.
8 1.0 0.619 0.622
8 1.3 0.433 0.434
9 1.0 0.753 0.756
9 1.3 0.580 0.584

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they differ from the values of bssd by at most 0.004. The print method summarizes the posterior with 9 events:

fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.753
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.522, median 1.438, 95% interval (0.379, 3.143)
fit90 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                     pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), level = 0.90)

The posterior mean of \(r\) is 1.52, and the article reports 1.53. The article gives (0.52, 2.83) as the 95% interval of \(r\). This agrees with the equal-tailed 90% interval, (0.51, 2.82), which level = 0.90 gives, and the equal-tailed 95% interval is (0.38, 3.14).

Example with subject-level data

The following data are simulated with sim_blinded() under the placebo distribution and the largest study drug distribution of scenario 6 in Table 1 of Duncan (2026). The 150 subjects are randomized 1:1, they enter the trial uniformly over 26 weeks, and each subject is followed for up to 104 weeks. The time to the event has a log-logistic distribution with \(\sigma = 0.8\), for which the hazard first increases and then decreases. The cumulative incidence at week 104 is 3.5% on placebo and 18.1% on the study drug. The blinded analysis is at week 117, the third interim analysis in the simulations of the folder reproduce of the installed package.

set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
head(d[, c("id", "entry", "follow_up", "event", "event_time")])
#>   id     entry follow_up event event_time
#> 1  1 14.446685  102.5533     0         NA
#> 2  2  3.150173  104.0000     0         NA
#> 3  3  3.683752  104.0000     0         NA
#> 4  4  3.806313  104.0000     0         NA
#> 5  5  9.020966  104.0000     0         NA
#> 6  6  1.833814  104.0000     0         NA
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
#>     exposure time_at_risk      n_event 
#>     15096.61     14605.76        14.00

The column group of d holds the true treatment group, which the blinded analyses do not use.

The data are analyzed with the four models of Duncan (2026). Their priors of the placebo parameters are based on historical placebo data with the event rate \(\lambda_{HP}\) and the total patient time \(PT_{HP}\), discounted by the factor \(DF\). The priors follow the simulations in the folder reproduce: a historical placebo group of 75 subjects, the size of the current placebo group, followed for 104 weeks and discounted by \(DF = 2\). For BDRIBS and EXP_BERN, \(\lambda_{HP}\) is the constant hazard per week that gives the placebo incidence at week 104, and \(PT_{HP}\) is in patient-weeks. For LL_BERN, the Gamma priors of \(\mu_p\) and \(\sigma_p\) have the means mu_hp and sigma_hp, and pt_hp divided by df_p sets their precision. The simulations use the historical patient time in patient-years for it. For LL_BERN, the relative risk is the ratio of the cumulative incidences at the time \(t^* = 104\); Duncan (2026) does not state which relative risk is used for this model, and ?llbern_post describes this choice and the priors.

lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2, t_star = 104),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                        t_star = 104),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                          t_star = 104),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
model prob signal rr_median ip_placebo ip_drug ip_difference
BDRIBS1 0.791 FALSE 2.879 0.053 0.118 0.065
BDRIBS2 0.805 FALSE 3.031 0.053 0.124 0.071
EXP_BERN 0.820 FALSE 3.243 0.052 0.131 0.079
LL_BERN 0.935 FALSE 4.217 0.041 0.152 0.111 
sig <- res$model[res$signal]

The column prob is \(P(RR > 1 \mid \mathrm{data})\). Models with a signal at the threshold 0.95: none. The relative risk is the rate ratio \(r\) for the BDRIBS and EXP_BERN models and \(RR(104)\) for LL_BERN. The table shows its posterior median, because the posterior mean of \(r\) is infinite for EXP_BERN under the default Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior of \(p\) (see ?expbern_post). The last three columns are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 104 and of their difference. The true values are 0.035, 0.181 and 0.146.

Accuracy of the numerical integration

bdribs_post() integrates over one dimension with stats::integrate(). The other functions use Gauss-Legendre and Chebyshev quadrature on a region located by a coarse grid (llbern_post() in four dimensions, multibin_post() and the Poisson likelihood of canary_post() in one, and the others in two). With control$check = TRUE, the default, they repeat the computation on a finer grid, return the finer result, and report an estimate of the integration error of prob, for example for the data above:

vapply(fits[c("EXP_BERN", "LL_BERN")], function(f) f$integration$error,
       numeric(1))
#>     EXP_BERN      LL_BERN 
#> 1.180896e-07 3.733315e-04

The number of nodes can be changed with control. ?llbern_post explains why the error estimate of LL_BERN is twice the difference between the two grids. sim_oc() turns the check off by default to save time.

Operating characteristics

sim_oc() simulates trials with sim_blinded(), applies the selected models at each analysis, and returns the proportion of trials with a signal and the posterior mean of the difference in the cumulative incidence. The example below uses the BDRIBS models with 200 simulated trials to keep the run time short; the column se is the Monte Carlo standard error of prob_signal. The cumulative incidence at week 52 is 10% on placebo and 20% on the study drug, 350 subjects enter over 26 weeks, and the analyses are at weeks 26, 52 and 78.

rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
design <- list(n = 350, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
               analysis_time = c(26, 52, 78), dist = "exponential",
               par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
oc <- sim_oc(n_sim = 200, design = design,
             models = c("BDRIBS1", "BDRIBS2"),
             priors = list(bdribs = list(lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52),
                                         pt_hp = 175 * 52, df = 2)),
             t_star = 52, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(oc$summary[, c("analysis_time", "model", "prob_signal", "se",
                            "mean_ip_difference",
                            "mean_observed_difference")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
analysis_time model prob_signal se mean_ip_difference mean_observed_difference
26 BDRIBS1 0.095 0.021 0.060 0.026
26 BDRIBS2 0.115 0.023 0.067 0.026
52 BDRIBS1 0.050 0.015 0.055 0.071
52 BDRIBS2 0.130 0.024 0.073 0.071
78 BDRIBS1 0.045 0.015 0.054 0.093
78 BDRIBS2 0.120 0.023 0.076 0.093

The true difference in the cumulative incidence at week 52 is 0.1. The column mean_observed_difference is the mean difference between the proportions of subjects with the event in the two groups at the analysis, computed from the true group assignment. The scripts in the folder reproduce (system.file("reproduce", package = "bssd")) run the simulations of Duncan (2026) for all four models with 1000 trials per scenario.

Reproduction and validation

The installed package contains the scripts and the results of the reproduction of published results (folder reproduce) and of the comparison with independent computations (folder validation). Each item is judged as PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a difference whose reason is registered), FAIL (a difference without a registered reason) or INFO (no value to compare with). The numbers of items are

file PASS EXPLAINED FAIL INFO
reproduce_Brock2023.csv 55 0 41 0
reproduce_Duncan2026.csv 15 6 0 7
reproduce_Duncan2026_prior.csv 23 6 0 0
reproduce_Duncan2026_simulation.csv 14 4 0 113
reproduce_Goren2020.csv 12 0 0 0
reproduce_Goren2020_table2.csv 120 0 0 0
reproduce_Gould2017.csv 71 17 0 0
reproduce_Mukhopadhyay2018.csv 82 4 0 1
reproduce_Schnell2016.csv 27 3 1 16
reproduce_Schnell2016_table1.csv 2 4 0 0
reproduce_Waterhouse2022.csv 11 0 1 2
validate_bdribs_package.csv 35 0 0 0
validate_convergence.csv 19 0 0 0
validate_gould2017_author_grid.csv 28 0 0 0
validate_jags.csv 24 0 0 3
validate_jags_methods.csv 16 0 0 1
validate_methods_python.csv 246 0 1 0
validate_sim_oc.csv 29 0 0 0

The reproduction covers Table 1, the hypothetical examples and the operating characteristics of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), Table 1, Figure 1 and the simulations of Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026), and the published results of Schnell and Ball (2016), Gould and Wang (2017), Brock et al. (2023), Goren et al. (2020) and Waterhouse et al. (2022). Many simulation results are INFO, because the articles do not report all settings of the simulations and some published values are read from the figures. The validation compares bdribs_post() with the bdribs package; the other posterior functions with MCMC in JAGS (for canary_post(), with the Poisson likelihood) and with independent Python computations (an exact finite mixture for binbeta_post()); the default integration grids with finer grids; and sim_oc() with an independent Python simulation. The number of FAIL items is 44. The files README.md and results/SUMMARY.md in each folder describe the scripts, the tolerances and the reasons for the EXPLAINED items.
